why_angle: The two cited pages show specs only. Neither lists a price or a cost per Wh, and neither covers the Anker SOLIX S2000. No page in the set says that Anker's own store charges the same $699.99 for the 2,010 Wh S2000 as for the 1,024 Wh C1000 Gen 2. That works out to $0.35 per Wh against $0.68, and it moves the car-camping pick. On 2026-11-13 I re-opened the maker pages to check the prices and specs, and Jackery's own help-center page confirmed its 70% cycle endpoint.

page.title: Power Station for Outdoor Camping: Energy per Dollar Compared (2026)
page.h1: Which power station for outdoor camping gives you the most energy for the money?
page.desc: Anker's S2000 sells 2,010 Wh for the same price as the 1,024 Wh C1000 Gen 2. We compare cost per Wh, weight, solar input and cycle ratings for camping.
page.answer: Short answer. For outdoor camping by car, pick the Anker SOLIX S2000 portable power station: 2,010 Wh for $699.99 at Anker's store, the same price as the 1,024 Wh Anker Solix C1000 Gen 2, so $0.35 per Wh against $0.68. To carry farther, the 25 lb BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 is $0.49 per Wh.
page.after:
What the differences mean

  • Cost per Wh at the makers' stores (2026-11-13): S2000 $699.99 ÷ 2,010 Wh = $0.35; Elite 100 V2 $499 ÷ 1,024 Wh = $0.49; C1000 Gen 2 $699.99 ÷ 1,024 Wh = $0.68; DELTA 3 Plus $719 ÷ 1,024 Wh = $0.70 (EcoFlow lists it as a sold-out pre-order).
  • Energy per pound: S2000 2,010 ÷ 35.7 = 56.3 Wh/lb; Jackery 1,070 ÷ 23.8 = 44.9; C1000 Gen 2 1,024 ÷ 24.9 = 41.1; Elite 100 V2 1,024 ÷ 25 = 41.0; DELTA 3 Plus 1,024 ÷ 27.6 = 37.1.
  • Fastest solar refill at full rated input (a lower bound): Elite 100 V2 and DELTA 3 Plus 1,024 ÷ 1,000 W = 1.0 h; C1000 Gen 2 1,024 ÷ 600 W = 1.7 h; Jackery 1,070 ÷ 400 W = 2.7 h; S2000 2,010 ÷ 400 W = 5.0 h.
  • Fridge nights from measured energy (a fridge averaging 40 W): S2000 about 1,900 Wh ÷ 40 = 47 h (Notebookcheck); DELTA 3 Plus 910 ÷ 40 = 23 h (StorageReview); Jackery 910 ÷ 40 = 23 h and C1000 Gen 2 890 ÷ 40 = 22 h (OutdoorGearLab).

Price per Wh: what the S2000 trades for its capacity

Anker's US store lists the S2000 at $699.99 (original price $999.99) and the C1000 Gen 2 at $699.99. That is the same money for 2,010 Wh against 1,024 Wh. Notebookcheck (Marcus Schwarten, EU 230 V unit) drew just over 1,900 Wh from the S2000 at about 250 W. That is roughly 95% of the label, so the extra capacity holds up under load. The S2000 is also rated for 6,000 cycles to 80%, against 4,000 to 80% for the C1000 Gen 2.

What the S2000 gives up for camping:

  • No 12 V car socket. Anker's own comparison table marks the S2000's 12 V DC port as "No". A 12 V compressor fridge needs its own AC adapter to run from the S2000. The C1000 Gen 2 has a 12 V 10 A, 120 W outlet.
  • Slow solar charging. Notebookcheck's datasheet lists 400 W solar input, so a full refill takes at least 5.0 h of full sun.
  • Less output. It is rated at 1,500 W against the C1000 Gen 2's 2,000 W.
  • No expansion. Anker lists the battery as not expandable.
  • Weight. At 35.7 lb it is 10.8 lb heavier than the C1000 Gen 2.

Idle draw matters if you leave the inverter on overnight. Notebookcheck measured the S2000 losing just over 10% of its charge per 24 h with AC on and nothing plugged in, about 8 W. The Solar Lab measured about 13.8 W on the C1000 Gen 2, which is 138 Wh over a 10-hour night. These are different labs, and the S2000 figure comes from the EU 230 V unit. {buy:anker-solix-s2000}

If you need to carry the station from the car to the site, the Elite 100 V2 is the better buy per Wh in the 1 kWh class. It costs $499, $200.99 less than the C1000 Gen 2 at the two makers' stores, takes 400 W more solar input, and BLUETTI rates it for 4,000+ cycles to 80%. {buy:bluetti-elite-100-v2}

Not recommended: Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 for long-term solar or car recharging

Jackery's own help center rates the Explorer 1000 v2 for 4,000 cycles to at least 70% capacity, not 80%. Its allowed fade is 30% ÷ 4,000 = 0.0075% per cycle, against 20% ÷ 4,000 = 0.005% for the Anker, BLUETTI and EcoFlow units. Its car input is limited to 12–16 V at 8 A (12 V × 8 A = 96 W), and Jackery gives around 12 h for a full charge from the car socket. Its 400 W solar ceiling means at least 2.7 h to refill. In its favour, OutdoorGearLab measured 910 Wh usable and said its fans stayed nearly silent even near maximum output.
